speechtext: that the first report of the standing committee on industrial relations, presented to the house on Thursday, February 25, be concurred in.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move an amendment to this motion, but before doing so I wish to say a few words in explanation.
On Thursday last, February 25, the standing committee on industrial relations met for organizational purposes. There was no definite agenda before the committee, and there was discussion as to the advisability of requesting from the house the right to sit while the house itself was sitting. The hon. member for Essex East made a motion-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I must question whether it is proper to refer to what took place in committee before the committee has reported. I
suppose this is a report of the committee, and in so far as what the hon. member is saying relates to this report it would be in order. Perhaps there is some contrary view. I just raise the question.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I appreciate your remarks, Mr. Speaker. If I understand correctly we have now a motion before us for the adoption of a report. This motion is, I submit, a debatable one. The report itself contains two items. One has to do with printing, and the other is a request to sit while the house itself is sitting. I am endeavouring to keep my remarks in line with the second item, to wit, the right to sit while the house is sitting.
The hon. member for Essex East expressed the view that if the committee should sit while the house is sitting it should study the problem of unemployment. The Conservative members of this committee were in favour of a request to sit while the house is sitting, but they, and especially the hon. member for Essex West, opposed the motion to study unemployment.
In dealing with this request to have the standing committee sit while the house is sitting I should like to refer to Hansard of February 15, 1954 at page 2102, where the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who was then the private hon. member for Prince Albert and a member of the opposition, had this to say:
A committee set up to study and report on unemployment would hear evidence of those who are warning this government and the country of the need for action now.
If this suggestion the present Prime Minister advanced at that time, was standing on only one leg, it is surely standing on two legs today when we have twice as much unemployment as we had at that time.
The motion before the house now seeks to grant the standing committee on industrial relations the right to sit while the house is sitting. We have no objection to this provided that the committee studies the problem of unemployment which has reached a state of national emergency.
I propose to move an amendment, but before doing so I should like to appeal to the Prime Minister and to each and every hon. member of this house. Let us take this golden opportunity to instigate action. This may be the last opportunity we will have during this session. We should not only grant this

Industrial Relations Committee standing committee the right to sit while the house is sitting, but at the same time we should empower it with full authority to investigate the most serious domestic problem facing Canada today.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc):
That the said report be not now concurred in, but that it be recommitted to the standing committee on industrial relations with instruction that they have power to amend the same so as to recommend that the committee not sit while the house is sitting until the definite subject of unemployment is referred to it for study.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have been asked to accept an amendment which to my mind is out of order. It is open to the house to amend the motion to accept the report of the committee which is before the house. The report of the committee reads in part as follows:
Your committee recommends:
1.	That it be empowered to print, from day to day, such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee, and that standing order No. 66 be suspended in relation thereto;
That is one part. The other part reads:
2.	That it be granted leave to sit while the house is sitting.
As I understand the procedure it would be in order to adopt the report in part or to amend the report within its terms, but the rule of relevancy applies equally to a motion to amend the report of a committee as it does to any other amendment. The proposed amendment goes beyond the committee's report, in that it seeks to give a new instruction in these words:
-that they have power to amend the same so as to recommend that the committee not sit while the house is sitting until the definite subject of unemployment is referred to it for study.
That is attaching a condition to the acceptance of the second paragraph of the report. If an instruction is to be given to the committee, notice of it will have to be put on the order paper and the motion moved in the ordinary way, because it is an originating motion, unless it can be brought within the four corners of the rule of relevancy that I have suggested.
That is my view of this amendment. Before dealing with it I should be glad to hear any hon. member who feels that the rules support a contrary view.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to speak to the point of order and bring to Your Honour's attention one or two points which I believe are relevant. While Your Honour has said that the motion is out of order, you have not given the citation or the standing order under which the hon. member's amendment is out of order. Your Honour has simply said that
[Mr. Deschetelets.l

the amendment is out of order; that it goes beyond the committee's report and that it attaches a condition to a paragraph of the report, notice of which must be given. It is with that statement of Your Honour that I respectfully take issue.
My reasons for stating that this amendment is in order are first of all that it does not go beyond the terms of the report made by the hon. member. It does not go beyond them because it offers in amendment to the two things which are under discussion and which are now before the house, namely power to print a certain number of copies and to sit while the house is sitting, that the power be taken by the committee not to sit while the house is sitting until such and such a thing is done.
What I should like particularly to bring to Your Honour's attention is the motion made by the Prime Minister himself shortly after the establishment of those committees, which I think is germane to the issue. The motion was the following:
That the standing committees of this house be severally empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
And so on. What the hon. member is doing now is amending the motion before the house to send this report to the committee and give it the powers that the Prime Minister moved in the motion he made following the establishment of the committees. Therefore, having regard to that motion, the amendment of the hon. member is in order.
There are other points, but I will not take the time of the house to deal with them now; they are contained in citation 291 of Beau-chesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", fourth edition. They are also contained in May's sixteenth edition at page 605, which I will not read because I do not want to take up the time of the house unduly. But I do say that all these citations, sir, point to the fact that where wider powers are being given-and that is not the intention of this amendment; this amendment simply refers the matter back to the committee for consideration of the direction that it should not sit while the house is sitting except to consider the subject of unemployment. The Prime Minister, when he sat in opposition, spoke to a motion by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Green). So that I will not be accused of misquoting I shall quote from what the Prime Minister said at page 2103 of Hansard of February 15, 1954:
After all, we are $10,000 a year men and women now, and would welcome all the worth-while work we can get to do. A committee such as this-

That was a committee on unemployment.
-would make a sphere of endeavour available to members that could not but be advantageous, that could not but bring forth suggestions which the government might find helpful to meet a situation which is becoming worse.
Then he went on to say:
We are not trying to build up fears that will bring on a depression. What we are trying to do is have parliament make a contribution now, to the end that we shall be able as a nation to compete in the markets of the world and thereby assure employment to Canadians in Canada. That is the purpose of this amendment, and it was in that spirit we moved it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, I expect that the citations Your Honour clearly had in
Industrial Relations Committee mind when you first raised the question will now be under your hand; but perhaps I might be permitted to take a moment or two to refer to them and to refute the attempt by the hon. member for Laurier to apply a completely inapplicable precedent, in which attempt, however, he was neatly exposed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The two principles which I submit make this amendment clearly out of order at this time are those regarding relevancy of amendments and that new matter cannot be raised except on a distinct motion after notice. You will agree, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed amendment is not relevant to the motion before the house and, further, that it is so irrelevant that it raises an entirely different and new proposition which can only be properly raised by motion after notice. In that regard I would refer Your Honour to citation 203 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 171, which in subparagraph 1 reads as follows:
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto.
Then to complete the exposure of the attempt made by the hon. member for Laurier to apply as a precedent for this situation, an amendment made on a motion to go into supply, Beauchesne continues:
The exceptions to this rule are amendments on the question of going into supply or ways and means.
So I do not think I need say more. I do not really believe that the hon. member himself thought he would get away with it. With regard to the question-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Now, with regard to the question of relevancy, Mr. Speaker, the same citation, subparagraph 5 reads:
An amendment was ruled out because it raised a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice.
I submit that applies to this amendment. What this amendment actually seeks to do is to give the committee new instructions. It is not amending the motion to adopt the committee's report, it is an attempt to give the committee new instructions and new powers. The amendment says-I had better read it.
That the said report be not now concurred in, but that it be recommitted to the standing committee on industrial relations with instruction that they have power to amend the same so as to recommend that the committee not sit while the house is sitting until the definite subject of unemployment is referred to it for study.

Industrial Relations Committee
You will recall the principle, Mr. Speaker, that the moving of instructions to a committee is a matter that requires a motion, which motion can only be moved after due notice has been given. I have not been able in the time at my disposal to put my hand on the specific rule, but it is found in that part of Beauchesne's fourth edition starting at page 236.
Now, the very fact that many of these motions have been required to stand instead of concurrence being granted later that day when the committee first reported is the result of this rule that no motion of such importance as this may be brought up in the house and debated on the same day it is first moved because, in fairness, the house requires notice of any such proposal. Since, therefore an attempt is being made, under the guise of an amendment to the motion to adopt the committee's report, to give the committee specific and further instructions, then of course that is an attempt that must fail; because it would be an attempt to take the house by surprise by debating a motion of which the house has not had adequate notice.
I submit, therefore, that on both branches- that the amendment is not relevant to the motion before us, and that it raises a new matter which can only be brought before the house on a distinct motion after notice- the amendment is out of order.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, what the Minister of Justice has said does not shed much light on the point about which Your Honour asked the house for its views in connection with the decision that confronts you. I thought at first the Minister of Justice was going to discuss whether this particular motion was debatable. However, since there is now no argument on that point we can address ourselves to the main consideration; that is, whether or not the amending motion is relevant to the main motion. The main motion is a motion for concurrence. The amendment is certainly relevant to the motion for concurrence as it sets out the circumstances under which that concurrence is acceptable to certain hon. gentlemen.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to note the form of the amending motion. It is drawn according to the form outlined for motion No. 95 which will be found on page 397 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. I am sure Your Honour, when he looks at the form of the motion contained on page 397 of Beauchesne, will see the force of the argument I have just put forward. We are adopting this particular procedural technique because under the rules

relating to standing committees of the house it is not possible for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision.
The committee on industrial relations in its first report seeks leave through the chairman to sit while the house is sitting; and the decision, as I say, cannot be reversed by the committee itself. My authority for that statement is citation 322, which will be found in Beauchesne at page 251 of the fourth edition. Citation 322, to which I have just made reference, provides a way out of the difficulty that confronts a committee once a decision has been taken by it, and that is by a decision of this house, instructing the committee to reconsider its decision, in this case restricting the sittings of the committee while the house is sitting to those occasions when the committee of the house is dealing with the subject of unemployment, which is the particular instruction which we wish the house to give at this time.
The report of the committee with which we are asked to concur is to be found at page 200 of Votes and Proceedings for last Thursday, and in the report the following appears:
Your committee recommends:
1.	That it be empowered to print, from day to day. such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee, and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto;
2.	That it be granded leave to sit while the house is sitting.
I submit to Your Honour that the amending motion is quite relevant to the second recommendation of the committee's report. The effect of the amendment is simply to restrict the sittings of the committee on industrial relations while the house is sitting to sittings dealing with the subject of unemployment. The house is asked in this motion for concurrence to grant the committee leave to sit while the house is sitting, and the amendment limits the application of that leave to sittings of the committee dealing with unemployment.
If Your Honour has any further doubt, may I put this question. Would it not be possible in an amending motion to restrict such sittings of this particular committee while the house is sitting to certain days of the week? That surely would be relevant, and if that would be relevant it is relevant too, I suggest, that this house has the power to instruct this committee to sit, under certain circumstances, on certain days of the week or in respect of a certain subject matter.
That is the submission which I make to Your Honour, with much confidence in its validity. I also refer Your Honour to citation-

Mr. Speaker, all I can say-this has nothing to do with my procedural argument-is that I welcome my hon. friend back to the house, and I only hope that his few days' rest, during which he doubtless had some academic tuition, has made him more mellow and on that account more constructive.
May I refer Your Honour to citation 220, subsection 2 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which says:
On May 5, 1893, the Speaker of the Commons of the United Kingdom laid down the following rules with reference to the instructions: "The principles which guide a limit in the system of instructions on going into committee may be thus stated: First, an instruction must empower the committee to do something which the committee is not otherwise empowered to do."
So I suggest to Your Honour that by the mere fact that this is a debatable motion, and therefore amendable, it must mean that the house is capable of putting forward an amendment; and there is nothing in our general rules permitting debate on this kind of motion which limits the form of the amendment in the way in which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has sought to do in the argument he has presented.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for these reasons and those enunciated by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), I submit to you with great respect that this amendment is in order. If you so determine this amendment will afford the industrial relations committee the opportunity to do some useful work in respect of a serious problem now facing the people of Canada.

I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that the reference by the hon. member for Laurier to May's sixteenth edition was a reference to the committee of the whole house and instructions that might be given to a committee of the whole house; and if Your Honour refers to pages 501 and 502 of May you will find those instructions are

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just say a word on this motion. When the Minister of Justice said a while ago that this amendment was irregular because it brought up a new matter, I think he was slightly mistaken. The amendment is to the effect that the report be not now concurred in, but that it be recommitted to the standing committee on industrial relations with the instruction that they have power to amend the same so as to recommend that the committee do not sit while the house is sitting. That is the main point. The hon. member who brought it forward did not ask the house to instruct the committee to go forward and study the whole matter of unemployment. Mr. Speaker, would you allow me a further word. In the Canadian Commons Journals, volume 65 for 1928, reference is made to the same situation. If I may just state the weight of the ruling, which by the way was also by an outstanding Speaker, it was to the effect that the house can always refer a report back to a committee with instructions to amend the report in any particular. In this particular case, the particular is the right to sit while the house is sitting.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I accept much of what has been said, but the problem is to apply it to this particular proposed amendment. I was taken by the force of the argument of the hon. member for Essex East that if the amendment were to the effect that the committee might sit while the house is in session, except for example on Tuesdays and Thursdays, that would be an appropriate amendment to refer back to the committee for consideration.
But that is not what we have before us, and if I accept this amendment it seems to me that I am opening up a debate on the unemployment question and the necessity

Industrial Relations Committee for discussion of that question by this committee, which would be quite beyond the scope of anything the committee has reported. The committee has not mentioned in its report any subject matter with which it has dealt or refused to deal, or what it proposes to do when it resumes its sittings. So there is nothing in the report about unemployment or the committee's consideration of that subject to which to attach this amendment. If it is relevant it must be attached to the committee's recommendation that it should have power to sit while the house is sitting.
If we were to accept this amendment we would in effect be saying, "You may sit while the house is sitting, but you may not do so unless you study the subject of unemployment". That in effect is the negative of this recommendation; and if it is the negative, then citation 202 of Beauchesne makes it clear, particularly in paragraphs 12 and 14, that such an amendment is not in order. Paragraph 12 reads:
An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage, is out of order.
Paragraph 14 says:
An amendment which would produce the same result as if the original motion were simply negatived is out of order.
The amendment does not go quite that far, but it instructs the committee that before it can sit while the house is sitting it must have undertaken a study of unemployment. That is what I read in the latter part of the amendment; that the committee shall not sit while the house is sitting until the definite subject of unemployment is referred to it for study.
The original terms of reference to the committee seem to be broad enough to give the committee power to undertake a study of unemployment if it feels disposed to do so. What we are asked to do by this amendment is to alter the terms of the instructions as to what the committee may study, or at least in relation to the times at which it may make its study; and that to my mind is irrelevant to what the committee has reported to this house.
I should like to refer hon. members to citation 203 of Beauchesne, particularly paragraph 3:
An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.
And to paragraph 5, which reads:
An amendment was ruled out because it raised a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice.


I think it is open to the hon. member who moved this amendment to put a motion on the order paper to instruct the committee to deal with the question of unemployment. That motion could then be brought up and debated. However, I do not think he can introduce it as an amendment to the motion before us because it goes beyond the terms of the report and constitutes, in effect, a new instruction to the committee as to what it must discuss. I therefore rule it out of order.

As soon as the supplementary estimates have been concluded-and I would have thought they would have been concluded long ago-then it is the intention of the house leader to introduce the agricultural estimates. In any event it is the intention to introduce them on Friday. When they are introduced I will then do that which I have been looking forward to doing for the last two or three weeks; that is, give an answer in detail, together with the reasons and arguments in support thereof, something I cannot do other than when debate is permitted.

speechtext: A supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister tell the house why he did not take the course he has taken on previous occasions, namely make his statement on motions, thus keeping his promise to the farm delegation instead of repudiating another promise?

I am to have the opportunity of presenting the views of the government on the agriculture estimates, and I shall do it at that time. It would have been done previously if it had not been for the hold-up of the work of the house on the part of hon. members opposite.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the delay in filling wheat delivery quotas on the prairies because of shipping priorities given to damp grain from northern areas, can the minister tell this house when greater movement of dry grain can be expected so that the present 3 and 4 bushel quotas may be filled?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The bulk of the damp grain in western Canada eligible for delivery under the advance delivery quotas of a 6 bushel maximum authorized by the Canadian wheat board has now been largely delivered. Indications are that there is very little damp grain eligible for delivery under this policy left on farms in western Canada, and that the problem of the prompt movement of this grain for drying at the terminals has largely been solved.
With the expectation of an early opening of navigation, plans are now being completed to resume the shipment of dry grain to the lakehead to meet sales commitments. To the extent possible the first priority for the movement of the dry grain will be from delivery points which are still on 1 and 2 bushel quotas. When these 1 and 2 bushel quota points have been raised to a higher level, then the shipment of dry grain from the points currently on 3 and 4 bushel quotas will be authorized.
In so far as shipments to Pacific coast ports are concerned, shipments of dry grain will continue to be authorized along with shipments of as much tough and damp grain as the drying facilities of the terminal elevators can handle.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister say whether there will be continuing
79951-0-100
Inquiries of the Ministry priority to elevator marketing points in southern Saskatchewan where quotas generally have been low, particularly because of the discrimination at the end of the last crop year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there was no discrimination last year in the bad sense of that word. Every effort is being made this year to equalize the quotas in so far as it is possible across the prairies, and special attention is being given to those few stations which remained on the 6 bushel quota last year and did not reach the 7 and 8 bushel quotas as the other stations did.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Transport. In the light of the visit made by an official of the Department of Transport to Dorval airport recently, at which time he stated in effect that there was no doubt whatever that the building would be completed on time but that it was another matter as to when operations would commence, can the minister say when this is likely to take place?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transporf):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: We expect to have people moving into the airport next September, and that is our hope.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: Has any decision been made in connection with the bar?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I thought I might get that question one of these days from the hon. member. The answer is that at large airports, where total employment may number in the thousands and where several score of private businesses may be carrying on activities, the department's role is primarily that of a landlord in relation to both land and buildings. The department expects the private businesses which are established on airports to carry on their activities in accord with provincial and municipal law.

The matter of a liquor licence would, in accordance with this concept, be left entirely to the restaurant concessionaire to decide upon and, where permissible under local law, to apply to the necessary provincial authority if a liquor licence is desired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question. Why did it take a year to make up your mind on this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMMENCEMENT OF OPERATIONS
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, Dorval airport will not be ready for occupancy until well on into the year, and I think this gives the concessionaire there plenty of time to make application if he so desires.

Since we have been refused permission this afternoon to discuss the problem of unemployment before the industrial relations committee, we are now bound to carry on the discussion of this most serious and grave problem before this committee of supply. It is true, as the Prime Minister stated earlier this afternoon, that

we are now entering the sixth day of debate on this particular item having to do with payments to provinces under the municipal winter works incentive program for 1959-60 and 1960-61 fiscal years.
When this item was introduced on February 9 and debated again on February 24, the Minister of Labour took time to inform the committee on the policy supposed to have been adopted by the government under this particular program to ease the serious unemployment situation. Unfortunately most of the time was taken up by a manipulation of statistics and percentages, and even by a reference to what the government was supposed to have done to take care of the serious unemployment situation since it took power over two years ago.
While this debate was taking place, while suggestions were being offered by the hon. member for Essex East, by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and by other members of the opposition, the committee was denied definite information. Following a precedent set by the Prime Minister himself, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, by the Minister of Transport and by the Minister of Justice with reference to the Jacques Cartier bridge, the Minister of Labour saw fit to keep this committee in the dark by refusing to give information on the actions of his own department, and particularly about measures being taken to find, if possible, a satisfactory solution to the seasonal unemployment problem.
Earlier this afternoon the Prime Minister stated that during five days of debate the opposition has been unable to supply anything. Well, Mr. Chairman, we got very little from the Minister of Labour. This committee will be interested to learn, not from the Minister of Labour, not even from the Prime Minister but from the premier of New Brunswick and from the minister of labour for Nova Scotia, that a joint federal-provincial economic study of seasonal employment problems in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia will be commenced in the next few months. Now, Mr. Chairman, the announcement of this step is being made to the house not by the Minister of Labour, not by a member of the government, but by a member of the official opposition.
This committee will be interested to know that through the Minister of Labour an offer has been made to undertake, in co-operation with the provinces mentioned, a thorough joint economic study and analysis of our seasonal employment problem, with the cost being borne on an approximately equal basis by the federal government and the government of the two provinces involved. This, Mr. Chairman, is pure mockery of parliament
Supply-Labour
and is typical of the attitude taken by the present government on matters of this nature and on matters of primary concern to the Canadian parliament. I welcome the announcement made on Friday last by Premier Flemming of New Brunswick and by Hon. Stephen Pyke, the minister of labour for Nova Scotia. This economic study of seasonal employment problems is directly in line with the suggestions made in this house by the hon. member for Essex East and turned down by the Minister of Labour.
The hon. member for Essex East went even further and asked for a more definite commitment when he asked for a federal-provincial conference with labour and management taking part. We want today to know the details of the Minister of Labour's proposals which were made to Nova Scotia and to New Brunswick which he refused to divulge to this house. We as members of parliament have a right to know what is going on.
Mr. Chairman, in the last two or three sessions, on most occasions when hon. members from the Atlantic provinces dared to exercise their duties as members of the opposition and offered criticism of the policies or lack of policies on the part of the present government, they have been called to order or accused by government members of running down their provinces and of being prophets of doom and gloom. The members of the present government are so embarrassed by their promises that they become reluctant to consider constructive suggestions made by opposition members.
The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond speaking in this debate on Friday last accused us of exaggerating unemployment figures and even of misrepresenting them. We are using figures which are supplied to us by the Minister of Labour himself and by the dominion bureau of statistics. Are we exaggerating, I ask, when we say that there are today in the vicinity of 135,000 unemployed in the Atlantic provinces representing between 11 per cent and 12 per cent of the labour force? Are we exaggerating when we warn the government about the unemployment insurance fund, which from $916 million in 1955 is down to $445 million as of January 31 of this year, and will probably decrease to close to $350 million by March 31? Are we exaggerating, I ask, when we claim that the present winter works program is inadequate, not practical and does not meet the needs of the serious unemployment situation? Are we exaggerating when we claim that the present government is not keeping its promises which it made to the unemployed of this country during the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns?

Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Yes, you are exaggerating.

The people of Canada know we are not exaggerating. The 800,000 unemployed today know that we are not exaggerating, but we do realize that you were exaggerating when you made those promises. Hon. members on the other side may boast about the fourteen new industries introduced in Nova Scotia in the last three years.
Hear, hear.

I hear "Hear, hear". But we do not hear one word about the larger number of industries which have closed down during the same period. Can hon. members boast about the Nova Scotian coal production which has decreased by 1,300,000 tons in the last two years? Is this the promise which was made by their party to the coal miners of Cape Breton in the last election campaign? The Minister of Veterans Affairs will not boast about the number of industries in New Brunswick which have dropped from 1,077 in 1952 to 975 after seven years of Tory government.
I agree with the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond that since 1957 a great many of the young people of the Atlantic provinces stay at home and swell the labour force. The hon. member, to use his own words, said that these young people know there is new hope in their province and in the other Atlantic provinces. I agree that they have been given new hope by the Tory promises of 1957 and 1958, but the main reason they stay at home today and swell the labour force is because not only is there no work for them at home, but if they dared travel to Quebec or Ontario to get work they would be forced to beg their way back home because unemployment today is at a high level even in those two central provinces. Our young people cannot live on hope alone; what they want is work.
We heard a lot about decentralization of industry. We have been told that we have yet to see a member of the Liberal party rise in his place and say that research centres, and so on, should be taken out of the central provinces in order to be established in the maritime provinces or in the western provinces. We opposition members from the Atlantic provinces are outnumbered by government members in the ratio of three to one, but have we heard one government member from these provinces even suggesting to the government that the nuclear research centre or other crown agencies should be established in the Atlantic provinces? No. The promises which they made were made outside of the house and do not mean a thing today. They

were selling the people of the Atlantic provinces, as was said by one of their own members, a bill of goods which they have failed to deliver.
Mention has been made of the defence contracts for the city of Halifax and Nova Scotia. The city of Halifax has today more unemployed than at the same period last year. I want to warn the government that in cutting defence expenditures the Nova Scotian labour force will be so seriously affected that the government will be compelled to find new industries to absorb the men displaced by defence cut-down.
Even the Minister of Veterans Affairs was scandalized and amazed the other day when on Friday, February 12 last, I mentioned the high unemployment figures ini New Brunswick, figures which have increased considerably since that day; as was also the Minister of Labour when I drew his attention to certain projects which could alleviate the situation in my own constituency of Gloucester. On that occasion I was accused by the Minister of Veterans Affairs of not getting up and speaking for my constituency when I was sitting on the government side of the house. I challenge the minister to look at the record. If he does he will find that in 1954 I spoke on 30 different subjects and in the session in 1955 I spoke on 24. Every time we criticize the government we are blamed for making personal attacks on ministers of the crown.
Notwithstanding what has been said on the government side as of January 31 of this year there was, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, 504,000 unemployed in Canada. There were 782,000 registered for unemployment insurance benefits; there were
786,000	unplaced applicants, 125,000 of which were in the Atlantic provinces alone; and as I said earlier this number has increased considerably since. There are today over 40,000 unemployed in the province of New Brunswick alone. This is not, as was said the other day by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, only picking up monthly statistics. The program which we have now before the house is insignificant and does not meet the problem of unemployment.
I have here an editorial from La Presse dated January 20, 1960.
I should like to bring to the attention of the committee one or two paragraphs from this editorial. It has as title:
(Translation):
Is that seasonal unemployment?
Hardly a few weeks ago, In their year-end surveys or New Year messages, federal and provincial ministers promised prosperity all around with an optimism that each of us was only too eager to share. However, that optimism was

dealt a rather shattering blow by the latest unemployment statistics, issued yesterday. And yet they are only the early winter figures, covering only the period from mid-November to mid-December. And the picture is darkest in the province of Quebec.
Farther on, the editorial says:
Over 12 per cent of Canadian workers have no steady job or no job at all. Is this not much too high a figure in a country which is considered prosperous? Especially if we consider that the position has certainly deteriorated since mid-December, and will continue to deteriorate until spring.
And still farther, we read:
True, the situation is slightly less serious than last year. But the improvement is far from satisfactory. The number of unemployed remains abnormally high. The comparisons being made in government circles, in an effort to brighten the picture, are strangely shaky. To prove that things are getting better, the present position is compared to that of a year ago, and last year to the year before, although 1958 and 1957 were recession years. It is quite a distortion of the truth and of the facts this attempt to suggest that all goes well, because things are not quite as bad as in bad years.
And the article concludes:
What about the famous winter works program in all this-the one that the federal Minister of Labour had talked about so much? It was of little help last year. And now, we hardly ever hear anything about it. Nothing was said about it in the speech from the throne, where unemployment was referred to only incidentally, as if it did not exist. Is the government going to wake up to reality?
I have here another editorial published in La Presse, dated December 17, 1958. It is entitled:
Federal winter works assistance program a huge hoax.
Those were the words of the mayor of Shawinigan.
(Text):
Whose responsibility is it to find a cure for this unreasonable, this serious, unemployment situation? This government was assigned this responsibility at the last election by the electors of Canada. It was assigned this responsibility because it had made certain promises. Those promises should be kept. I would remind the committee of the promise made by the Prime Minister in Welland on March 21, 1958 when, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of March 22, 1958:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker today promised jobs -not relief payments-for Canada's unemployed.
We don't want relief-that's why we launched this public works program," the Progressive Conservative leader said, referring to the works program the government says will total $1,185,000,000 this year.
And the Prime Minister went on:
"I hope that by June or July the application of our policies will have met the problem, through 79951-0-101
Supply-Labour
loosening tight-money and through public works, so that no one will be suffering from unemployment."
The Prime Minister should be the last person to mention loosening tight money in the light of the money situation today considering the all-time high interest rates. Then, speaking in Halifax on March 24, 1958, the Prime Minister was reported as follows in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald:
His government was launching "one of the greatest public works programs this country has ever seen" in order to stimulate employment. "I am able to tell you that we're over the peak as the result of our policies. I can see the light ahead and employment reasonable and complete, over the next few months."
That was two years ago, and today we are facing a situation where 800,000 people are unemployed in this country. Then the Prime Minister continued:
"I know what unemployment is. They don't have to tell me second hand," he added. "But as long as I am Prime Minister, deficit or no deficit, no man or woman is going to be allowed to suffer because of unemployment," he pledged.
These are words which have been quoted very frequently in this house. I should like the Prime Minister to go into certain sections of my constituency and neighbouring constituencies and find out, not at second hand but at first hand, what is going on. There is dissatisfaction with the policies of the present government so far as unemployment is concerned. I have here an article from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of January 18, 1960, which has for title: "Labour Council 'Dissatisfied' with Prime Minister's Action." It reads in part:
The New Glasgow and District Labour Council is completely dissatisfied with the action taken by Prime Minister John Diefenbaker regarding the employment situation in Trenton plants, it was learned at an executive meeting of the council held Sunday.
"It is only right that the Prime Minister give immediate attention to this serious problem which exists in Trenton" Council President Warren Riggs said Sunday night. "And by the letter received from him this week, it is obvious he is not going to do anything about it at the present time."
I have here another article from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald dated January 22, 1960. It has for title "Thousands Jobless in Shining Sixties". Here is a further article from the Toronto Star dated January 28, 1960. It has for title "How Many Without Jobs?" I should like to put on record the paragraph from this article which reads:
With roughly one in nine persons on the nation's labour force seeking jobs, this could be regarded as one of Canada's most urgent problems. Yet, except for an occasional outburst in parliament, the politicians remain unperturbed, the government is doing little, and there is a minimum of public outcry. It is only the long lines that form at dusk before the institutions offering free bed and meal that provide any evidence of distress.

Supply-Labour
Yet in the face of all this the Prime Minister is accusing us of taking the time of the house in order to discuss unemployment.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

When I have finished my remarks. We are only allowed a limited time in which to speak. I have here a letter from the United Steelworkers of America, local 1231, Trenton, Nova Scotia. It is dated January 19, 1960 and it is signed by the financial secretary. I will not take up the time of the committee by reading the whole of this letter, but the second paragraph says:
Some of the privations brought to our attention are unbelievable in a country such as Canada. We have 1,200 men idle and hundreds of them have no regular or seasonal insurance credits.
What is the attitude of the present government toward this unfortunate situation which exists in the maritime provinces? I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg South, speaking in this chamber on February 5, as reported in Hansard at page 805, said:
-even at their present rates of pay, in certain regions of our country that rate of pay, being equalized as it is across the nation, is deemed probably by civil servants to be adequate. I think that civil servants who are employed in Newfoundland and the maritimes would feel that they were being reasonably well cared for.
There is the attitude of the government. They want to differentiate with regard to the residents of the maritimes. This exemplifies the attitude taken by the government -that though we in the maritimes are struggling to meet high living costs brought on through exorbitant municipal taxes and transport charges we should be satisfied to receive less income than the other sections of the nation.
Suggestions have been made by the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and by a number of other hon. members on the opposition side but the Prime Minister said this afternoon we are offering nothing to settle the problem.
I have in my hand an article to which I should like to direct the attention of the committee. The article is entitled "To Live or to Die" and is taken from the February issue of the Atlantic Advocate. I wish to place on the record the following paragraph:
Here in the Atlantic provinces is an ideal opportunity. There will be plenty of others in other parts of Canada; hut let us take for examination our own Atlantic area where the need is great.
We are worse off than the rest of Canada by more than a third. Pledges have been made to rectify that disparity. The Atlantic resolutions promised help. The Gordon royal commission recommended it. One of the measures common to both was the establishment of a capital projects commission.

Such a commission could be set up with a directive to carry out full-scale engineering studies of various proposals that are being advocated and have long been advocated by the governments and business groups of the region.
I leave this thought with the government for consideration. If I had sufficient time at my disposal I would suggest to the government through the Minister of Labour various measures which even in my own constituency of Gloucester would alleviate the unemployment situation to a great extent.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Mr. Chairman, I will answer questions when I complete my remarks.
There is, for example, construction of public wharves which provide facilities to fishermen. They enable fishermen to increase their production and create additional employment on shore. This year the estimates show a reduction of $30 million with respect to the construction of wharves, harbours, et cetera, $3 million in New Brunswick and $2.5 million in Nova Scotia. When the government provides fishermen with such facilities we can be sure that production will increase and additional work will follow.
I wish to bring to the attention of the government what is being done in Europe today. This should give the government some food for thought. In the United Kingdom the development areas policy introduced during the depression years is now being extended to cover almost one fifth of the nation's population and in the last 15 years has provided work for more than half a million displaced workers who were able to find jobs in their home towns or regions.
The tax exemption and direct grants plan introduced in the southern half of Italy, together with rail rates reductions for the moving of produced goods, have resulted in an uplift for the area and have provided opportunities for the establishment of new industries. Special bonuses or initial investment grants granted by the French and Dutch governments to industries establishing in recognized backward areas have succeeded in bringing back those areas in line with more fortunate sections where industries were already established and operating at full capacity.
Only recently the Belgium government introduced exceptional measures to assist the coal mining areas which were facing problems quite similar to those affecting the coal industry of Nova Scotia today.
The policy adopted by European countries not only promotes the economic expansion of

regions where industries are lacking, but also acts as a brake on the further development of already over-industrialized areas.
Areas like the Atlantic provinces are not begging for hand-outs or ad hoc measures which could provide nothing but temporary relief. What we need now are fundamental measures such as tax concessions, low cost loans and an adequate freight rate deal, measures which could attract some industries which are today being establish elsewhere in this promising country of ours.
In conclusion I say that the Atlantic representatives should unite and with one voice insist on something exceptional, something which has already been described as being of a scope this nation has not attempted before. Surely what Europe is doing Canada can do. It can be done in this country of ours where our national resources are practically untouched and still remain an attraction for unlimited development. Regional retardation in Canada should not be permitted and means should be taken to bring about a lasting solution to existing conditions.

Mr. Chairman, would the
hon. member permit a question before he resumes his seat? In his remarks the hon. gentleman referred to unemployment in Trenton and generally in Nova Scotia and the maritime area. During the past year some 47 million tons of freight passed through the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland ship canal.
Question.

Mr. Chairman, we have had

This vote provides $15 million as a payment to the provinces for one half of the cost of labour for approved winter works projects under the federal-provincial program. Hon. members of the opposition have characterized this $15 million payment by Ottawa for winter works projects as peanuts. As the Minister of Labour has pointed out, the provision of 40,000 extra winter jobs is not "peanuts".
The minister has stated he hopes that the final payment by Ottawa may be as much as $25 million. This will depend on the initiative of the municipalities and the provincial governments. It is up to the municipalities and provincial governments to arrange for projects under the terms and conditions in the dominion-provincial agreements, and then Ottawa will pay half the cost of labour. In my constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre this program has provided jobs and thus helped in some worth-while undertakings.
I am thinking of one particular instance, namely the assistance given by this program to much-needed improvements to one of our fine parks which is such a tourist attraction in the summer. Most of the work on this project was done by day labour, which helped the local winter employment picture.
I mention winter works to lead up to a look at the possibility of greater winter construction by private contractors. In this connection, I should like to read a short excerpt from an article in the Globe and Mail by

Supply-Labour
E. N. Davis regarding winter work on the South Saskatchewan dam. Mr. Davis is an editorial writer for the Liberal newspaper, the Regina Leader-Post. In his own newspaper Mr. Davis writes editorials painting the darkest possible picture of unemployment in the west. In the Globe and Mail he tells this story about work on the South Saskatchewan dam, 75 per cent of the actual cost of construction being paid by the federal government. Here is part of his article:
Those who think that work on the $96 million South Saskatchewan dam stopped with the coming of winter would he due for a surprise were they to visit the dam site now.
They would see scores of mechanical earth-moving giants crawling over the wintry landscape. They would hear the sharp staccato beat of riveting hammers echoing up and down the valley.
Approximately 300 men are on the job. Some are operating and servicing the fleets of earth-moving machines used on the first phase of the east and west embankments. The remainder are erecting the steel superstructure for the construction bridge which will span the 800-foot wide channel into which the river has been squeezed, and which will link the operations being carried out on each side of the river.
Gordon Watson, engineer for the P.F.R. administration says the experience being gained on the dam confirms that this type of work can be carried out economically with heavy equipment, even if temperature drops to 40 below zero.
Paradoxical though it may appear, severe winter conditions have enabled the contractors to recover ground lost because of the unseasonal October blizzards; the project is back on schedule. The $8,500,000 federal vote for the job in the present fiscal year will be utilized in its entirety.
Present indications point to a federal appropriation almost double this year's $8,500,000, and a new peak of employment of approximately 300 men at work on half a dozen contracts.
Winter work in connection with the dam is going on in my own city of Moose Jaw. Commercial Shearing Limited of Youngstown, Ohio, and Hamilton, Ontario, were awarded a $2,787,250 contract for 550 steel rings for the five huge river diversion tunnels which will divert the river while the dam is being completed. The first steel has been unloaded at the Moose Jaw plant and 30 or 40 local men will get jobs. There will be additional trucking jobs to transport the steel rings to the dam site. My object in referring to the report on the work on the dam is to show that construction ideas and construction machinery are changing, and it is now possible for contractors to plan for more winter work.
I have watched with great interest the steel work going up on the 9-storey building on Metcalfe street which I pass every day on my way to this house. This work has been going on all winter and one can hear the riveting hammers going nearly every day. There could be many other such winter construction projects, I am sure. I think
fMr. Pascoe.]
this represents a challenge to construction firms, a challenge to put their building programs on a basis that will reduce the effects of seasonal winter unemployment that was just as bad, if not worse, when the former government was in power, and when much less government effort was made to solve the problem. 150,000	square feet. During this debate mention has been made of vocational training. Last year the Minister of Labour outlined what the federal government is doing in this regard. One of the measures we are taking is the technical and vocational training program now under way in co-operation with the provinces. Under an agreement signed in 1957, some $40 million is being made available to the provinces over a 5-year period for the establishment of suitable training facilities.
This is the federal program that is helping in a very big way the technical institute at Moose Jaw. A capital allotment of $1,470,300 from federal funds is being used for the building and equipment. This agreement extends for a 5-year period to March 31, 1962. The department of education through the federal-provincial special projects agreement announces a special winter training program for unemployed workers... at the technical institute, Moose Jaw.

and physically able to perform practical shop work. Trainees will be paid a nominal living allowance but are responsible for finding their own lodgings in Moose Jaw. This is just a brief outline of some of the efforts that the government is making to provide more employment in my area. I can assure the Minister of Labour that his assistance in this regard is greatly appreciated. Now that the winter is nearly over I think we have passed our worst unemployment period, even for the winter months in the years ahead. I am sure the Moose Jaw technical institute, built, as I have said, in very large part by federal government financing, offers a means for our young people to fit themselves for good jobs as the present economic growth continues. I can assure the Minister of Labour that his efforts and the efforts of the government to reduce unemployment are not regarded as "peanuts" in my constituency.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of the introduction of this item by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to say a few words on unemployment, not only in my area, but in the country in general.
I do not intend to weary the minister with statistics. I have just heard the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe) tell us all that the Minister of Labour has done in his attempt to relieve the acute problem of unemployment in this country.
The way we look at it, Mr. Chairman, is this. Whether there are five, six, or ten

Supply-Labour
children in a family, the ones requiring our greatest care and attention are not the healthy ones but those who are ailing.
I will not quote statistics to the minister because figures represent unemployed men, women and children. That is why I do not want to start an argument with the Minister of Labour, because it is about the plight of those people behind the statistics, people who are suffering, that we should do something.
I readily admit that the Minister of Labour has tried to do something. Even if we are in the opposition, we must at times, endorse measures taken by the government in its attempts to find an answer to our problems, but what worries me is that the answers offered, namely the winter works program to relieve unemployment, are not satisfactory. There are still too many unemployed Canadians and when I think of the solemn promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in this respect, I wonder if he can sleep soundly at night after promising Canadians that not a single citizen in this country would suffer from unemployment.
In Quebec, at the end of January 1960, nearly 250,000 unemployed had applied for U.I.A. benefits.
Mr. Chairman, there have been years of less unemployment. There were people affected at that time, but not so many as now. Yet, I remember how fervently and feelingly the present Prime Minister was urging the government to call a federal-provincial conference to consider a possible solution to the serious unemployment problem. If there ever was a time when we should ask that such conference be called, it is now when thousands of Canadians are trying to find a job and the means to earn bread to feed their wives and children. Consequently, I ask the Prime Minister to remember now the feelings he expressed when he was sitting on this side of the house, and, if possible, to give evidence of human sympathy by calling a federal-provincial conference to consider the unemployment problem.
I know that some hon. members from the C.C.F. tell us now and again that unemployment is hurting this country's production. Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that it is difficult to consider unemployment from the point of view of national production alone, without regard for the human element and the moral factors affecting men, women and children. There, I think, is our main reason for dealing with unemployment.

The leaders of the western democracies often tell their voters: "You know, we must get away from communism and from absolute socialism because we have moral, intellectual and spiritual values which should be prized above everything in this world". But, Mr. Chairman, it is not just a question of appealing to people's idealism in order to try and preserve our most cherished values. In addition to making them understand the importance of our ideals and our moral and intellectual values, the course we take must agree with the principles we preach and I think that unemployment is one of the worst evils in our society. That is why this government should not hesitate to do everything in its power to find an immediate solution to this problem.
The other day I heard the Minister of Labour reply to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who had made some concrete suggestions-and I admit that some of them were long-term ones-that his proposals could have no immediate effect.
But if year after year the Minister of Labour keeps replying that our suggestions cannot give results for years to come, what is he doing to provide now for the consequences of unemployment one, two or even three years from now?
To my mind, as he indeed informed the cabinet, the Prime Minister and the representatives of the C.T.C.C., some planning is required, and I am not afraid of the word planning.
Sometimes, I admit, when the word is used by socialists, it may have unpleasant connotations. But if we look it up in the dictionary, we find that the word planning means "to make plans for the future." I therefore unhesitatingly urge the government to plan for the future and to provide for one, two or three years from now.
In this connection, when look at the noisy and fallacious publicity of the Soviet union, I think that we are in danger of running into trouble here in Canada. Through its embassy here in Ottawa, the Soviet union is flooding Canada rwith publicity on all that happens and will happen until 1965 in the U.S.S.R. I have here a pamphlet on working hours, on the number of homes being built each year, and so on. About working hours, for instance, the Russians state the following:
(Text):
By 1966-68, all Soviet workers will be transferred to a 35-hour working week (five seven-hour working days), and workers engaged underground or

in trades injurious to health to a 30-hour working week (five six-hour working days).
(Translation):
There are people here in Canada who quote this material in support of the statement that we are not doing enough for our own people. They forget to tell Canadians, however, that such a program, if it is ever implemented in Russia, will be put into effect at the expense of human dignity and personal freedom. We must prevent such propaganda from taking root in the minds of Canadians who are suffering from our own system at the present time.
I am convinced that our system is one of the best, if not actually the best. But it has certain shortcomings which we must hasten to correct. If we cannot agree on a two- , three- or four-year policy, we must be prepared to make the necessary sacrifices to find more than mere stop gaps to unemployment, although I am not in favour of full employment-I do not believe in it-even if the theory exists; it is all well and good to preach integral employment or the theory of full employment, but I do not believe that such a thing will ever be possible. However, there is a percentage below which we must not drop.
Too many Canadians today are suffering from unemployment. We must do more than we are doing today. I hope the Minister of Labour is listening to what I have to say and will not accuse me of making politics, because I am trying to deal with the matter in terms of the human problem involved.
Like many other members of this house, when I am through with politics I shall be able to make a living elsewhere, perhaps better than I am doing here. For the time being, I am simply trying to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to the human problem which is involved in unemployment, and to ask him to stop flinging statistics at us, to say that there are 10,000 or 5,000 less unemployed than there were last year, or that there are more Canadians at work. It is not those who have jobs who deserve our sympathy; they don't need it; they are making a living. Let us save our sympathy for the unemployed.
Even if 40,000 Canadians were given jobs through the winter works program, what about the 600,000, 700,000 or 750,000 others who are jobless? What about the other thousands who are not getting any unemployment insurance benefits?
I believe those problems not only deserve our sympathy, but call for concrete measures on the part of the government, who should

try to solve them. I am not telling my colleagues in the house anything new in saying that prolonged unemployment only breeds misery among its victims and their dependents. Unemployment also undermines the courage of its victims. And anyone whose morale is affected-

He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all I thank the house for consenting to having these bills dealt with first. The present application is an application by the parent Swiss reassurance company, which is the largest reassurance company in the world. It has at present a subsidiary in New York in the United States, the North American Reassurance Company. Private Bills
business directly to Canada, which will mean a head office being set up in Toronto and a transfer of a payroll of roughly $120,000 to $150,000 per year to the benefit of Canadians. The proposed manager of the Canadian branch will be a Canadian.
This company, of course, is applying primarily for the right for reassurance work, although other powers are asked for in the charter. The proposed company will have an authorized capital of $3 million. It will commence business with a subscribed and paid-up capital of $1 million, and in addition a paid-in surplus of $1 million, thus bringing roughly $2 million for investment in Canada.
This company, of course, is being formed in compliance with the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, which is chapter 31 of Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, as amended in 1957. If you recall the amendment in 1957 it provides that at least the majority of the directors must be Canadians, and this will naturally be complied with because it is the law of the country. I also stated that the company will be managed by a Canadian who has been trained in New York and is returning to Canada to carry out the operations of the company. If the house sees fit to pass this bill and it goes through the normal processes of the committee, the company hopes to start operations at the beginning of May of this year. He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill asks for the incorporation of the Munich Reinsurance Company of Canada with head office in Montreal. The Munich Reinsurance Company of Germany, a joint stock company under German laws, was founded in Munich in 1880 with the approval of the royal Bavarian government and is now the second largest reinsurance company in the world. It is a professional reinsurance company engaged exclusively in reinsurance.
In order to extend and organize its business abroad, and because the needs of overseas markets can only properly be met by local

organizations, the Munich Reinsurance Company has since the end of the last century transacted business in the United States through a branch office. In Canada the Munich Reinsurance Company opened a Canadian branch office under the management of Sterling Offices of Canada Limited in Toronto in November 1957.
The Munich Reinsurance Company of Canada will have a capital of $1 million and a surplus of a further $1 million fully paid up. The Munich Reinsurance Company of Canada will transact both Canadian and foreign reinsurance business of every description with the exception of life business. The board of directors will be composed of nine gentlemen of whom, in accordance with the legal provision, at least five will be Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In this case I am wondering whether the hon. member who was the chairman of the committee can give us an assurance that there had been no opportunity for collusion, and that this was a straightforward case?

I think I would not give that assurance in any case. All I or any member of the committee can do, or the people in the other place who heard this case, can do, is to look at all the evidence and make a decision as to whether the grounds for divorce have been met and whether the case is a good one or not. I do not think that anybody can ever give the assurance asked for by the hon. member. 1 think it is more likely that there was no collusion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in asking this question I have in mind something that the Prime Minister said the other day in referring to the capital punishment debate. He said that all hon. members must take a moral and an honest position to see that legislation that is passed is what it appears to be. For this reason I believe we should be careful to make sure that Bill No. SD-11 has no collusion

attached to it. I say this because, as I have already stated, a reputable man has written a letter that would indicate that somebody this year is going to pay $1,200 to the House of Commons or to the other place, and is going to obtain a divorce which the parties have committed collusion to get.
I agree the hon. member should not have to say there was no collusion in this case or in the other. His assurance will certainly, in my opinion, strengthen the reasons for getting this particular bill through the House of Commons. If hon. members have all given as close attention to this bill as has the chairman of this committee then maybe they themselves are going to be able to say, when they vote for one of these bills, that it is a good case and no collusion took place here. As conscientious members we should ask these questions. We do not suggest that the hon. member answering the questions on behalf of the committee should have to say whether or not collusion did take place. If he gives us the assurance that it is not a likely case where it did take place, certainly I am happy to take his word for it. In this particular case were detectives used to establish the evidence?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, detectives were used. I thank the hon. member for his kind words, and would point out to the committee that one can establish a lot in these cases by the advantage of seeing the parties before the committee. This, of course, happens in the committee of the other place. Many of these gentlemen have the advantage of a great number of years of experience in hearing these cases. They have the advantage of looking at the parties, particularly the petitioning husband or wife, and knowing whether they are giving straightforward evidence, or whether there is something sneaky about the way in which the whole matter has arrived in Ottawa.
For example, I had the opportunity of reading the evidence of the wife since the hon. member started to ask questions about this case. I had read the evidence before; I read it again. She is in her mid-twenties; she seemed to establish a very solid ground for her divorce with the committee of the other place, and she painted a picture of the relationship when she and her husband lived together, which was not a happy one.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in this particular case the sponsor of the bill has mentioned that this was a very young couple. The husband was not old, either; the lady was in her twenties. In this particular case did the committee make any effort to effect a reconciliation rather than passing this relief measure?
Private Bills-Divorce

Yes, indeed; this is one thing we can say about our colleagues in the other place. Wherever it is possible they will ask a great number of questions, or suggest to the people concerned that they consult family counsellors or their ministers. There were quite a few questions asked by Hon. Mr. Gershaw who, as I think everybody knows, has a tremendous reputation across Canada for trying to patch up these unhappy marriages that come before the Senate and the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am pleased to hear this because I did not know before that the other place had this service. I think it is an advantageous one. If this young lady had brought her case before a provincial court rather than bringing it to the House of Commons she would not have had the benefit of that type of service, and I am quite pleased to know that the Senate has now decided to supply that.
In view of the fact that consideration has been given to reconciliation in this case, did the detectives appear as stupid as they usually do or was it a clear-cut case where evidence was presented that might indicate that there had been some collusion, particularly in view of the fact that the Senate thought that there might be a possibility of some understanding being arrived at?

I think the evidence in some cases is gone into very thoroughly from the point of view of the course of the investigation before entry is made into the hotel or motel. In this case that did not happen. I think that once the committee had heard the wife's story of the unhappy marriage with her husband they were quite prepared to get down to the bare bones of the evidence that was required to round out the story. They did not require very much more and I must say that I agree with them.
