speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
How was admittance to the
apartment gained?

Detectives had watched
the place in question on two prior evenings.

On the third evening the first detective called the second detective who arrived on the scene about 9.30 in the evening. Around eleven o'clock or 11.30 at night the two detectives went to the apartment and pressed the buzzer on the door. The gentleman inside happened to be a doctor. They said, "Doctor, this is an emergency", and he opened the door and they went in.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That was very handy but we
are speaking of detectives who I presume are licensed people and who are supposed to have some ethics. Is there no question in the mind of the sponsor about accepting testimony of this nature from people who have admitted that they have lied?

The hon. member has hit
a gold mine in this question. I am sorry that I inadvertently misled the committee when I said that they were detectives. These two gentlemen have appeared in quite a number of cases but they call themselves insurance investigators. I do not mind naming them for the record. One is George Rolland Foucher, 43, of Montreal, and the other is Don Kennedy, 29, of Montreal. For some years they have been coming before these committees of parliament and giving evidence in divorce cases. They have investigated these cases. I think the hon. member heard them give evidence in a case that was heard by the miscellaneous private bills committee. There is a problem in the fact that these people have not taken out licences to be detectives in the province of Quebec.
I have had some discussion of this matter with the chairman of the committee of the other place and we hope that some friendly persuasion will lead Mr. Foucher and Mr. Kennedy to mend their ways. It is quite true that because they are not licensed detectives they are not liable to certain penalties that could be applied by the provincial authorities. The hon. member has a good point. It shall be pursued.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I had not realized that Kennedy was one of the men involved in this case. Now that it has been brought to our attention I think I may say that members who were on the committee a year or two ago were very unimpressed with his ability as a detective and were very impressed with his ability to deal with the truth very loosely. He had a very short memory and every time he had to call on his memory the result was different than the time before. Because of the reputation of these gentlemen I would assume that we should give much closer study to this bill

than we would have otherwise. In view of the fact that these gentlemen's names have been mentioned, I would suggest that the sponsor of the bill could not assure the committee that there was no collusion in this case. Because this detective agency is not licensed and because the word of these men is unsupported in the main except by people who have no more character than they have, I would think that this could possibly be the case we have been looking for. This may be case that appears in Liberty magazine in the form of a letter. I would suggest that we are going to have to give closer attention to it. I should like to ask the sponsor of the bill, through you, Mr. Chairman, if the committee of the other place asked for any verification of the charge of adultery, other than the unsupported testimony of these detectives.
Some slight evidence on the part of the petitioner, Mr. Chairman, to the effect that it was quite probable her husband had, in fact, committed adultery.

As a point of interest, Mr. Chairman, is the copy of the evidence from which the hon. member is reading the same as that which is available to the sponsor of the bill? I do not mean to indicate I do not enjoy the exchange of views across the floor, but I think the hon. member has the same evidence as is available to the sponsor. I would suggest, that if he wishes to challenge any of these divorces on the grounds of collusion, the proper way would be for the committee to have the Minister of Justice intervene rather than to waste a whole hour on these divorce matters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am really surprised at this intervention. The hon. member is suggesting that we have not the right, in this committee, to question any of these bills.
He did not.

I was not suggesting you had no right to intervene in this particular bill. I was suggesting you have the same information available as the sponsor of the bill. I know he can read, and I suppose you can too.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not believe it matters whether or not I can read. I do not think this is the point in question. The problem is that these bills are going through this committee, and they are not being sponsored by me. They are being sponsored by an hon. gentleman who is quite capable of answering all the questions and who has done a remarkable amount of work on them. He has, I think, given the committee more information, and has given more study to these matters
Private Bills-Divorce
than any other chairman of the private bills committee. I have read the record for past years and noted the manner in which the divorce bills have been handled, the slipshod way they have been passed. I would suggest that the fact of whether or not we can read them is of no importance at all.
I think the sponsor of these bills is quite happy to justify them before the committee. The committee of the other place may be willing to grant relief to these people, but certainly no hon. member in this committee should have a hand in the passage of these bills if he has not given some consideration to them and does not know something about these particular bills. If there is any question in any hon. member's mind about any phase of a particular bill, then I think that hon. member has an obligation to the country- so long as we are handling divorces in this manner-to ask questions. I would think, therefore, that the fact of whether or not I can read is not of much importance. The fact of whether or not the sponsor of these particular bills is satisfied in all particulars is of importance to me and should be of importance to all other hon. members.
I suggest that hon. members of this committee who have heard detectives like Kennedy testify have an obligation to give very close consideration to any bill with which detectives of this type have any connection. I believe the private bills committee was of the general opinion that the evidence of such detectives

I think this can be checked- was very shady, very sketchy and their memory or loss of memory always suited their own purposes.
I do not believe it is of any importance whether or not the members have read the information adduced by the committee of the other place. Most of the witnesses do not appear before the private bills committee of this house, so we are depending entirely on somebody else's interrogation of the witnesses and we are giving consideration to a decision that was taken by other people. With this in mind, I would say we have an obligation to this committee; we have an obligation to the Canadian public in general; and we certainly have an obligation to the people who are involved in these divorce cases to ascertain whether or not there was any collusion or whether they are bona fide applications for divorce. I think we have an obligation to do this.
I am very happy that the chairman of the private bills committee who sponsors these bills is prepared to answer these questions. I am very pleased also that he is capable of answering them. He not only has read the

Supply-Labour
evidence, but in many cases he has sat in the committee of the other place and has had an opportunity of listening to and meeting some of these people. I am quite sure that if the hon. member who made the interjection were to ask the sponsor of these bills if he gave much credence to the evidence of the detectives in this case he would find that some of the evidence of these detectives is suspect, even in the sponsor's mind.
This raises another matter which I think should concern the committee. We have people coming before committees and testifying under procedures that would be considered other than the normal court procedure and where they do not have to be too worried about perjury. It has already been established, certainly in my mind, that they do not give much consideration to the truth. Some of them are more interested in making a fast buck by getting paid for the number of days they work on these particular cases. Some of these detectives have been in Ottawa on a number of cases and there are 500 cases to come before us. I feel we have an obligation to ascertain for ourselves if there have been any unusual circumstances arise in connection with the evidence of these detectives in the past and, if so, I think we should have the opportunity of calling these detectives who are operating on a continuous basis in divorce cases before our committee and requesting that they give us some justification for some of the evidence they present.
In this particular case, I should like to ask the sponsor how extensive was the time spent by these detectives on this particular case.
Six o'clock.
I can answer that very simply. They were in company together on three occasions and they had some other evidence to support the chain of conduct which I mentioned before.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, as I said when the house adjourned, young men and middle aged people who find themselves without a job for quite a long time, soon get demoralized and even end by feeling that they are useless in our society. While at first they think of themselves as unemployed, they soon come to look upon themselves as unemployable in the society in which they live.
Especially do our young people, Mr. Chairman, lose the best years of their lives trying to be useful members of society. They lose the best years of their lives when they should be trying to get settled and wield due influence as citizens in their community. In addition to losing their morale, our young unemployed may even become bad citizens in a society which almost rejects them; at least they think of themselves as being rejected by society when they are unable to find employment and earn a living for themselves and their families.
As I said this afternoon, what is important, serious and tragic in the unemployment situation, are the human factors. They are the factors we should consider. Human dignity is what we have to consider. It is with that situation that we must deal and we, as the representatives of the people have a very serious duty, I believe, in this regard.
In Montreal, His Eminence Cardinal Leger dealt with the matter last year when he reminded all representatives of the people, at the municipal, provincial or federal levels, of their duty with regard to this situation affecting a very great number of Canadian citizens.
I will quote only an extract of Cardinal Leger's letter, which was published in Saturday Night of February 14, 1959. About unemployment, His Eminence wrote;
(Text):
This evil afflicts a very large number of workers, brings misery to their families and seriously jeopardizes social order.
Who would dare to say. in the face of this situation, that all types of unemployment are normal, and at the most constitute a "neccessary evil?" Such a statement would be as little in agreement with the natural law as it is with the oresent-day science. A Christian cannot remain indifferent in a situation which creates such

great suffering. Behind the statistics and figures, we must discern the men and women, the children and the aged who are reduced to poverty and exposed to the terrible temptations of despair.
Deprived of the moral advantages which result from employment, the unemployed have the impression that they are no longer useful to society. This situation upsets family life and endangers the peace and harmony that should reign in the home. The head of the family is humiliated because of his inability to fulfill his family responsibilities; he feels that he is a failure. Discouragement can take hold of him, and his enforced idleness can expose him to all sorts of temptations. The increase of criminal offences in times of acute unemployment is a further indication of the gravity of the situation.
How can we reconcile the vision of thousands of citizens without work with the picture of a country which is immensely rich and in full development?
A recent report on the royal commission for Canada's economic prospects states that our country ''is one of the rare countries which can find, within its boundaries, the greater part of the primary materials which are necessary to any great industrial power, and since 1945 a great number of discoveries and developments have come up to make Canada still more self-sufficient ... Canada can consider itself particularly privileged and blessed among the other nations of the world."
A reform of the economy is necessary and it is possible. It is false to state that the economic order is affected only by certain mechanical influences, as it were, and that it follows certain inescapable laws which man is incapable of influencing. Economic life is the work of reason. It is certain that it has its own laws and its own exigencies, but by his free behaviour and the activity of his reason, man has the power to modify the operation of the economic structure and to direct it, with due regard for the particular circumstances of the times and for the common good of all.
(Translation):
I said earlier that the representatives of the people have a serious duty. But those who lead the government, who shape the destiny of our country, have an even more serious duty, because theirs is the responsibility of correcting the faults of our system.
In his letter to the archdiocese of Montreal, His Eminence Cardinal Leger gave some views about the duty of the members of the House of Commons of Canada. In concluding, I would like to read what His Eminence had to say about the duties of the representatives of the people in the House of Commons. Again, according to Saturday Night of February 14, 1959, he said:
(Text):
If I am a representative of the people, a city councillor, a member of the provincial government or federal government:
Do I realize the grave responsibility of my mandate in the face of present unemployment?
Am I convinced that "the state has the important mission to prevent any disturbance of the equilibrium of economy resulting from the conflicting interests of selfish individuals or groups?"
Supply-Labour
Am I convinced that "the state is obliged to protect the right to work of its citizens, (not in the sense that outside of a collectivist society it should itself furnish employment) but it must take care to diminish the rise of unemployment or at least to palliate its consequences by exerting influence on economic and professional organization whose autonomy, however, it must take care to respect?"
As a servant of the common good, have I always done everything possible to prevent, to delay or to ease this human suffering?

I made that as a practical suggestion and I should like to hear what the minister has to say about it. I also suggested that the capital grants commission which the Tory government promised for the Atlantic provinces should be established at once, and I should like to hear what the minister has to say about that. I also suggested that the program of the fisheries council of Canada with regard to fishing vessels should be put into operation at once, and I should like to hear what the minister has to say about that. I also suggested that the other Atlantic resolutions sponsored by the Minister of National Revenue should be carried out at once, and I should like to hear what the minister has to say about that, too.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Bonavista-Twillingate realizes very well that that is not a question of privilege. I would ask the Minister of Labour not to reply at this time. I recognize the hon. member for St. Mary.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, since I represent in parliament a riding where most people are in the ranks of labour I can state in this house that the workers of my constituency will never forget the poor representation given to them here by the Liberal party.
During the discussion on a Department of Labour estimate, we have witnessed tonight a most degrading scene for the Canadian parliament and the Liberal party. As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said earlier, Liberal members' speeches are less calculated to offer practical solutions to unemployment than to make headlines in the next day's papers.
I imagine that the Liberals are pleased when unemployment is mentioned in this house, but the happier they are to see people out of work, the more uneasy they will be after the investigation on the Jacques Cartier bridge.
Mr. Chairman, everybody knows that the Liberal party has never paid close attention to the plight of the working class, perhaps because they preferred to protect the interests of shareholders of the Rio Tinto Mines 79951-0-1021
Supply-Labour
Company, where they had a great many friends. They preferred to take this course rather than to look into the chronic problem of unemployment.
Everybody knows that when the Liberal party was in office, we had to wear ourselves out in order to earn a living. For the members of the Liberal party, the war was a stumbling block. The Liberal party never agreed to put before the house a practical policy to avoid a degree of unemployment such as we have had lately.
If my Liberal friends want to be consistent, logical and avoid big headlines in the papers, I would suggest that they refer to previous debates on unemployment.
I am sorry to see that there are here certain members who were in this House of Commons when the words I am going to quote were spoken and who never uttered a single word when the unemployment situation was being discussed. However, we now find that they are pleased to see the increase in the number of unemployed in this country and it is quite natural; they offer no concrete suggestion to correct the situation.
Mr. Chairman, if the Liberals really mean to be sincere, I would ask them to re-read what Mr. St. Laurent said in this house on February 20, 1950, as it is found at page 56 of Hansard, about a program put forward to solve the unemployment problem, and I quote:
And special inducements were proposed to make it financially advantageous for provincial governments and municipalities to co-operate in the shelf project and to co-ordinate the timing or execution of these public works. It was felt that with that kind of co-ordination it would be possible to time the execution not only of such projects as were of national concern but also of those which were local responsibilities of provincial or municipal_
Mr. Chairman, this is precisely the policy which the Conservative government is trying to apply. It is the policy suggested by their leader in 1950, though he did nothing about it. And today, those same people come here, in this house, to upbraid a government which wants to achieve what the former prime minister of Canada wanted to do to cure unemployment. That is the Liberal party, Mr. Chairman.
During the same debate, on February 27, 1950, Mr. Stanley Knowles asked the prime minister the following question:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will consider giving the house a statement at an early date as to the government's proposals for relieving unemployment.

Supply-Labour
This was in 1950, and Mr. St. Laurent answered:
X have nothing to add at the moment to what I then said.
That was the comedy and the blackmail which the Liberals offered the population as long as they were in power. Today, we see the opposition members rise in this house and behave like school children.
Now, I represent a constituency which is entirely a labour riding. Now that illegitimate child which has been named unemployment- was put into the world by those heartless fathers the Liberals, who tell us now: "You; the Conservatives, now have this illegitimate child and you have to bring him up!"
Mr. Chairman, I am not among those who profit from such deplorable conditions as unemployment by resorting to demagogy. Only, like my colleague, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Rieard) I am asking the following question: Why did the Liberals stress that unemployment insurance act formula so much in 1942?
In order to protect them from the Conservatives.

In order to protect the public against unemployment. But there was unemployment, when they were in power. I shall tell you what you have done. You have allowed the unemployment situation to become more serious. If statistics have to be quoted, may I give a few figures: for March 1950, as can be seen in the official record of this house-and I refer to a question answered by Mr. Cote, the representative of Verdun-Lasalle-the figures established for the period 1948-50, indicated an increase in the number of jobless people for each province in this country. If the hon. member who asked me this question would listen, I shall quote those figures:	In the province of
Quebec, there were on July 1, 1948, 29,000 unemployed; on December 30, 1948, there were 55,900; on the 30th of June 1949, when seasonal unemployment had somewhat abated, there were 42,400; on September 29, 1949, 43,900; on November 3, 1949, 51,900; on December 1, 1949, 67,300; on December 2, 1949, 88,200 and on February 2, 1950, 109,300.
Mr. Chairman, do not forget that it was the time of the stingy Liberal regime and that seasonal workers were getting no unemployment insurance benefits. Well, I say that under the Liberal administration, unemployment was more acute than it has ever been, under any administration.

We realize to what extent the Grits, who will always be oppositionists if they keep on behaving as they are now doing, are glad of an unfortunate situation. But do not forget that they are not improving the fate of the unemployed when they are talking that way in the house. At the next election, I shall remind my electors of the unfortunate speeches they made in this house about the fate of the unemployed.
In my opinion, we of the Conservative party are too conscious of our obligations and duties to make politics out of this unemployment situation. Our friends claim that there have never been so many unemployed than at present, but I have just showed them they are wrong in quoting figures which speak for themselves. If they will look up Hansard for June 19, 1950, on page 3838, they will read the following:
After all, there were some 425,000 Canadians who suffered from unemployment last winter, whether it was seasonal or whatever it was.
I would point out that this refers to 1949.
Those people are anxious to know If any steps are being taken to avoid a repetition of that situation again next winter. I suggest to the minister that it is not howling calamity to ask the government just what steps are being taken to avoid a repetition of that situation.
That, Mr. Chairman, was at the time of the former Liberal administration in 1950.
Well, Mr. Chairman, we realize to what extent our friends to the left are not sincere. They have (tried to fool the house in launching into a debate about Elliot Lake. I should like to associate myself with the hon. members who have expressed their sympathy to the people of Elliot Lake about the situation now prevailing in that city. If the Liberals thought they could raise these people against the government, they made quite a mistake, because last night I watched a people's forum on television station CJAD. In fact, it had been announced that the Elliot Lake situation would be discussed, and all listeners had been asked to phone in to the station and give their views on the situation.
I must say that despite the powerfully organized Liberal machine, the people were not taken in. The people who phoned the station said the Liberals were responsible for the present situation at Elliot Lake, and that the Conservatives should not be blamed. Mr. Chairman, I think the people will not be fooled by this kind of publicity and blackmail.

Again I say it is unfortunate that the opposition should be happy at the situation arising out of seasonal unemployment.
Sometimes I wonder, Mr. Chairman, how the Liberals can take such advantage of the generosity of the house in using three times as much time as the Conservatives to discuss unemployment. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the house shows great patience in putting up with it. Personally, I have had to wait six days before speaking. Opposition members prevented my speaking earlier. They acted so as to get the headlines in the next day's newspapers.
I realized that the Liberal opposition, for lack of something better, tries to prepare the Liberal provincial campaign on the question of unemployment.

On a point of order. The hon. member for St. Mary implies that he has tried for two or three sittings to take part in this debate and that the opposition has prevented him from doing so. I do not think it is-

I believe that the statement of the hon. member for St. Mary-
I would like to hear the question of the hon. member. Mr. Chairman, I am sorry, but I do not understand the intervention of my hon. friend.

speechtext: I do not quite see the point of order in the question of the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I understand his sensitiveness about that matter, and to avoid all misunderstanding about that, may I say that I have not been prevented arbitrarily, as it was done at the time of the Liberals. I say that the Liberals, under our democratic system, take three times as long to discuss the question of unemployment as any other party. This is what I meant.
May I come back to the matter under discussion. I said earlier, when my hon. friend was clever enough to interrupt me, that the Liberal members are trying to conduct in this house the political campaign of the provincial Liberal party. Since they have no leader, no program, they try to make the headlines by making speeches here in order to attract the attention of the population of Quebec which, however will ignore them at the next provincial election.
Obviously, they will do anything to create a sensation, but in addition to discussing the Jacques Cartier bridge, they should read and reread the statements made by their leader,
Supply-Labour
Mr. Pearson, in the Times for February 17, with regard to unemployment. I quote:
(Text):
It would be stupid and foolish to blame unemployment on the Conservatives.
(Translation):
And we heard the Liberals in this house say nothing but that the Conservative party was responsible for that unemployment situation.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the function of an opposition, I am quite willing to agree, is to criticize. But the question I should like to put to certain members of the opposition is: "What do you suggest?" And that, as the minister asked a moment ago, in order to try to improve that unemployment situation in Canada.
Not one of them has put forward any concrete solution, or even introduced any worthwhile suggestion. They all said: "Our function is not to make suggestions but to criticize. Well, the Liberals have no right to criticize when their fellow citizens have nothing to eat, they have no right to limit themselves to criticism in this house, because they represent the people. They have been elected to a function which should make them aware of their obligations towards the classes they represent. There are very few members in this house who do not have to represent the working class of their constituencies. Therefore, we urge them to be loyal and honest towards their constituents and to tell this house what they would suggest in order to alleviate the seriousness of this temporary situation of winter unemployment.
Let the province of Quebec pay half of it. There is a suggestion.

You have nothing new to offer. This government has already offered to pay on a 50-50 basis. The Conservative government has told the municipalities and the provinces: Undertake works programs and we shall pay half of the cost. Well, for the Grits to provide work for 30,000 people is not sufficient, they are not interested, they would just as soon have 30,000 more unemployed. In fact, they prefer that to providing employment, even for only 30 men. That is their way of thinking. They laugh and smile, they do not think of discussing the Jacques Cartier bridge, but only the employment situation.
I was listening to the hon. member for Laurier, (Mr. Chevrier) on television. It was on a Monday, I think it was about three

Supply-Labour
weeks ago. The hon. member for Laurier would probably remember the date better than I-in any event, it was on "Tribune Libre", and he said it was under a Conservative government that unemployment had been the greatest. You know how clever he is: he took the period from 1945 to 1955, and said that under the Liberal administration, unemployment had been only 2 per cent. Imagine that. The hon. member took a 10-year period, but he skipped the 1949 period, when there were 10.7 per cent unemployed people in Canada. The member for Laurier cleverly concealed from the people of Montreal what his friends knew about the unemployment situation when they sat together in the cabinet.
He said that the Conservatives had done nothing about unemployment. But, in his cleverness, he forgot to say that the Conservative government had launched a winter employment campaign; that it had increased unemployment insurance benefits and that it had decreased-a thing the Liberals never wanted to do-the number of immigrants admitted in Canada during the period of unemployment. This is something that the Liberals never wanted to do at the time they were in power.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder why the Liberals, who had better take care about the Jacques Cartier bridge, do not say in this house that the Conservative party has extended unemployment insurance coverage to include all the seasonally unemployed, like the fishermen, the stevedores, the farmers, the married women and many other groups. Those are things the Liberal party did not do. Besides, this government has extended the period of benefits, a thing these gentlemen opposite had refused to the population.
I do not wish to delay the debate, Mr. Chairman, but I only want to say, as a representative of the working class, that workers in my riding are very happy, that they put all their faith in the Conservative party and that they are not fooled by criticisms of the Liberal party because, in their opinion, it doesn't amount to much.
Knowing that our friends like to make a political issue out of unemployment, I should like to say that I am in favour of a more careful study of our legislation, with a view to taking some measure designed to avoid the seasonal unemployment that affects so many homes. Therefore, I urge authorities to call a federal-provincial-municipal conference where labour and management representatives, labour union and local chambers of commerce would get together to devise an acceptable plan to avoid the slack period that affects workers every year.
[Mr. Valade.l
Furthermore, I would like to suggest to the federal government, that loans to municipalities should be made at a reduced rate of interest, which could vary from 1 to li per cent, in order to facilitate the carrying out of necessary works.
This would induce municipalities to participate more actively in winter and seasonal works. Thus, we would contribute to the relief of unemployment, and our Canadian homes would be grateful not to the former Grit administration, which did nothing, but to the Conservative government which gave proper attention to the problem.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very surprised that many members of the house, during the last several hours when we have been discussing unemployment, have acted as though they were at a political circus or convention.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have been interested in a particular aspect of unemployment which has also come to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister recently. I refer to the area displacement problems facing a large number of sections of the country, and particularly the situation at Elliot Lake.
I took the opportunity to go to Elliot Lake last week. I understand that a number of ministers have been invited there. The Prime Minister has been invited. From headlines in the Sudbury Star I see that the Prime Minister and his wife may visit Elliot Lake shortly. I would strongly recommend that all members of parliament who are interested in area unemployment should go to that area and have a look at the town and the situation developing there. I think they will realize that this is a very serious problem, a problem that should never have been allowed to develop but now that it has developed we are going to have to do something about it.
I do not think it is good enough to say that the Conservatives are not doing this and the Liberals are not doing that. I do not think we should introduce political arguments relating to the hon. member who represents the riding concerned or the minister particularly concerned with the matter. I think we have to give very serious consideration to solving the problem and I suggest it does not really
Supply-Labour
matter what member of parliament makes a suggestion. He may only have an idea, but if we in Canada cannot sit down, collectively solve our own problems and arrive at a solution that can be implemented to alleviate a situation on which attention is focused by what has happened at Elliot Lake but which exists in many other areas, in fact, in all our primary producing industries and every mining camp ever developed in this country, then I suggest that we are not functioning as a very effective form of government.
I think we can give this kind of consideration if we quit bickering back and forth about who was responsible and decide what we are going to do because the problem is going to have to be solved and we may as well decide to do something about it. In speaking on this matter the other night I suggested that we should set up a national industry planning board with considerable authority and that such a board would be able to go into an area depressed by unemployment and assess everything on the economic side of the picture, all those things that were favourable and everything that prevented industry from settling in that area and making the community operate as it would if industry already existed there.
Elliot Lake probably deserves more consideration than any other town we have ever considered. It deserves it because we have been building Elliot Lake from the time we started natural resource development in Canada. The government of the day realized that mining there only had a five year life at a guaranteed price and that something would then happen. The price of the ore was either going up or down or there would be no contracts.
Elliot Lake is not a normal mining town but probably the most complete and modern city in Canada today. It is the size of North Bay and it has no old buildings. Every building in the town is new. Those who had shacks there before the development had to tear them down. I believe it is the most modern city of its size in Canada and probably anywhere on the North American continent. We built and established Elliot Lake. Government control was evident at all stages of the development of the town. Elliot Lake was developed because we needed atomic energy for defence. We needed material for atomic defence and there was co-operation. We had co-operation from the United States in building the town, and I think it is a credit to the Canadian people.
But it is no credit to the Canadian people if the citizens of this town are now thrown out of work and have to look for jobs in other communities and leave behind them five

Supply-Labour
years of their lives with nothing to show for it. I suggest that we can do something about the situation. I talked to an engineer at Elliot Lake the other day who told me that a small factory could probably be established immediately which would employ 50 or 75 people in the manufacture of toys and allied products from hardwood.
I hear some people saying, what an argument that is. We only need in that town enough employment for 9,000 people. It is quite likely that the whole 9,000 will not want to stay there. Some of the miners who have been making $12,000 and $14,000 per year are not going to be satisfied to remain in that town and work for wages which the industries will probably pay.
However, this is no reason for not establishing these industries or for not giving some assistance to the establishment of them. I am not sure just who those ladies from Elliot Lake were, but most of them were not miners' wives. They were the wives of businessmen, members of the chamber of commerce, church organizations and other organizations that are very concerned about this particular problem. They came to Ottawa and were particularly interested in having this research centre switched from Manitoba to Elliot Lake. I pointed out to a number of people with whom I talked that Manitoba may have some claim on this Whiteshell research centre. There may have been reasons for the original decision to locate it in that particular province.
However, I believe the government, and certainly the Prime Minister when he spoke to these ladies the other day, indicated that serious consideration would be given to this matter. I understand that these people have gone home and are telling other people that the Prime Minister is going to look after them. One woman who appeared on television said that a nice man like that would never let them down. The farmers of western Canada could tell them what this nice man could do and could not do. There have been other organizations that have come to Ottawa, the representatives of which are probably not as naive as some of these ladies from Elliot Lake. I would suggest that we cannot wait for somebody to fulfil promises about Elliot Lake. Now is the time to do some planning rather than to make promises. If we cannot solve this problem, then how can we run a country?
There are only 9,000 people concerned. There is a statement here as to how many houses there are in this town. It does not really matter how many houses there are. They are going to be there anyway. They are not going to be sold. Central Mortgage

and Housing Corporation is now requesting permission to rent these houses. I noticed that, according to the newspaper, eight holders of C.M.H.C. mortgages have walked out of their homes, turned the key and left. They are now being searched for by the officials of that corporation because they have left their mortgage and everything else and just walked out. There were 2,000 homes built under Central Mortgage there. We have this town, and I think the problem can be solved. It cannot be solved, however, if we are not going to face up to it.
I cannot see any reason why this matter cannot be referred to a committee. I do not understand why we could not have the best specialists in these fields give the government some assistance in setting up a board that would work, not only in the Elliot Lake area but if it were successful in Elliot Lake it would be able to re-establish industries in places like Cape Breton island and in other coal mining communities in the maritimes. I would suggest that we in northern Ontario, in the northern gold mining communities would be quite happy to give back to the Canadian people the money received through emergency gold mining assistance if some way could be found to use this money through a planning commission to bring industry into the area to satisfy the needs of our communities. We would rather have this plan than the continued bolstering of the mining industry through subventions and other forms of assistance because that industry may have passed its peak and become a liability rather than an asset.
I suggest this can be done, Mr. Chairman. If we have not enough brains in Canada to decide what industries could be brought into places like Elliot Lake for the least amount of money, then let us hire them from some place in Europe. I was very interested in talking with a gentleman the other day who has recently come from Europe. He pointed out that a great deal of development has taken place in West Germany. He said that this was not the result of the German people being smarter than anybody else but because they decided a certain thing had to be accomplished and they set out to accomplish it. After the war they had to re-establish industries where no industries existed. This gentleman then pointed out that the German people then did something we have never been willing to do. They hired the best salesmen they could find and sent them across the world to sell the industrial products which the country was beginning to produce. I believe we have capabilities which are equal to those of other countries.

I think we are going to have to realize that if we are going to plan the development of a town like Elliot Lake to produce war material then we are going to have to plan an economy for that area that will meet the needs of the area just as we did in the first place to get the uranium industry established. We can do this and I suggest that we will do this. I should like the Leader of the Opposition, who has a great interest in this particular problem, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce who also has a great interest in this particular problem, to go to Elliot Lake with me to debate this particular problem. Then the people of Elliot Lake would have an opportunity of knowing what they were going to get.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we will continue with our progress on the supplementary estimates. We have covered four items and we have 15 more to do. When that is finished tomorrow afternoon, early, then we will go on with the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the tenure of office of judges. I will list the other items with which we should like to deal as promptly as possible.
The last item would be followed by the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the National Housing Act; then, the motion in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to set up a joint committee to deal with
Business of the House
amendments to the Indian Act; then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with amendments to the Railway Act; and the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the Trans-Canada Highway Act. This would be the business for Wednesday and Thursday, in that order, unless something unexpected happens. On Friday we will commence with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and Monday and Tuesday of next week will be devoted to a supply motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might ask the house leader whether he has given any thought to the time at which we might resume the debate on capital punishment in which everyone in the country is so greatly interested?

speechtext: Yes, I recognize the interest, but I am not in a position tonight to name a date for that.
Can the minister say whether it may be sometime next week?

speechtext: As I say, I am not able tonight to name a date.

speechtext: May I ask if any further consideration has been given to taking the housing resolution before the matter of the Judges Act in the name of the Prime Minister?
